tours.name: The Hellgate
tours.blurb: Where the valley narrows to a canyon of wind — the old village, the young city, and a Pleistocene lake written on the hills.

keys.cap: Missoula, at the sheet's very edge — the 1912 quadrangle ends at the city's doorstep, the mills and the university just beyond the neat line.
Hell Gate, the original 1860 townsite — a trading post at the canyon mouth the Salish called the place of ambush. Five years later the town moved upstream to the mills.
Mount Sentinel and Mount Jumbo. Look closely at their flanks: the horizontal benches are the strandlines of Glacial Lake Missoula, drawn by two thousand feet of ice-dammed water.
The Missoula Valley — lakebed silt, now farms; when the ice dam broke, this basin drained toward Idaho in days.

tours.name: St. Mary's Mission
tours.blurb: The oldest permanent settlement in Montana — and the valley the Salish were made to leave.

keys.cap: Stevensville: St. Mary's Mission, founded 1841 at the Salish people's own invitation — the first church, first farm, first mill in what became Montana.
Saint Mary Peak over the mission valley — the Salish name for the river and valley meant 'place of the bitterroot,' the food and medicine plant that named everything here.

Fort Owen, the trading post that bought the mission buildings in 1850. In 1891 Chief Charlo's band was marched north from this valley to the Jocko — a removal the sheets record only as empty farmland.
Victor, named for the Salish chief who signed the 1855 Hellgate Treaty believing the Bitterroot would remain his people's home.

tours.name: Daly's Valley
tours.blurb: The copper king's other empire — stock farms, sawmills and an orchard boom on the valley floor.

keys.cap: Hamilton, laid out in 1890 by Marcus Daly to mill Bitterroot timber for the Anaconda mines — the biggest sawmill in Montana, and a town built to company plan.
The Daly stock farm — a thousand acres of thoroughbreds; Tammany's barn was finer than most houses in the county.
Corvallis and Woodside, heart of the apple boom — ten thousand orchard acres sold to easterners on irrigated promises; the frost of 1910 read the fine print.
Lake Como, dammed in 1910 to water the orchards — the moraine lake the Como Peaks hang above.

tours.name: The Wall
tours.blurb: Forty miles of granite canyons on the valley's west side — Leiberg mapped every burn and stand of it in 1898.

keys.cap: The Bitterroot front — a fault scarp of granite canyons, evenly spaced as organ pipes. Pull the layer slider to Leiberg's 1898 survey: greens for timber, hatching for burns.
Blodgett Canyon, the show canyon of the range — half a mile of cliff on either side, cut along a joint in the Idaho batholith.
Kootenai Creek, the trail canyon above Stevensville. Leiberg counted board-feet; the 1910 fires would recount them.
Saint Joseph Peak — snow saved into July, feeding the ditches that made the valley's orchards possible at all.

tours.name: The Lolo Trail
tours.blurb: The Nez Perce road over the mountains — Lewis and Clark westbound, and a fleeing nation eastbound.

keys.cap: Lolo, at Travelers' Rest — the Corps of Discovery camped here in 1805 and again in 1806; the site still shows their latrine's mercury.
Up Lolo Creek — the ancient Nez Perce buffalo road over the mountains, the worst eleven days of Lewis and Clark's whole journey.
Fort Fizzle, July 1877: soldiers barricaded the canyon to stop the Nez Perce; Chief Joseph's people simply climbed around them, and the fort earned its name.
Lolo Peak, the sentinel of the pass — the last Bitterroot summit before the trail drops to the Lochsa.
